The card lists N(B) = A, C, D and N(E) = C, D, F, G, and returns C and D." width="100%"} Returns the intersection of the two nodes' neighbor sets. Neighbors are taken with `mode="all"`, so in a directed graph a node counts as a neighbor of `node_1=` (or `node_2=`) if there is an edge between them in either direction. The number of common neighbors is one of the simplest and most effective structural similarity signals. Typical uses: - link prediction: two unconnected nodes with many shared neighbors are likely to become connected (the basis of Jaccard and Adamic-Adar scores) - triangle detection: if `node_1=` and `node_2=` are adjacent, each common neighbor closes a triangle with them - finding shared contacts, co-authors, or mutual friends The two input nodes themselves are not returned unless one is a neighbor of both (for example via a self-loop). The method does not modify the graph or the selection. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_1]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The first node, given as an integer node ID or a string label. An unknown ID or label raises `ValueError`. [node_2]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second node, accepted in the same forms as `node_1=`. The operation is symmetric, so swapping `node_1=` and `node_2=` gives the same set of nodes. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node IDs that are neighbors of both `node_1=` and `node_2=`. Built from a set intersection, so it contains no duplicates and its order is not guaranteed; sort it if you need a stable order. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Both "A" and "B" connect to "C" and "D", so those two nodes make up the intersection; "E", which only touches "A", is left out: ::: {#91e619fe .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) graph.add_edges([("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "D"), ("A", "E")]) common = graph.get_common_neighbors("A", "B") sorted(graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in common) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['C', 'D'] ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, edge direction is ignored: "M" is a successor of "X" but a predecessor of "Y", and it still counts as a shared neighbor: ::: {#f50133ab .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} digraph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["X", "Y", "M"]) .add_edges([("X", "M"), ("M", "Y")]) ) [digraph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in digraph.get_common_neighbors("X", "Y")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['M'] ``` ::: ::: A node sharing a common neighbor with one of its own neighbors is the signature of a triangle -- this scans every neighbor of "A" for exactly that pattern. The triangle A-B-C is found twice, once from each of its other two corners: ::: {#d2b42226 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "D")]) ) a_id = graph.get_id_from_label(label="A") triangles = [] for neighbor_id in graph.get_neighbors(node=a_id): for third_id in graph.get_common_neighbors(a_id, neighbor_id): triangles.append(( "A", graph.get_label_from_id(node_id=neighbor_id), graph.get_label_from_id(node_id=third_id), )) triangles ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [('A', 'B', 'C'), ('A', 'C', 'B')] ``` ::: :::
